ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial video-call style, with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A but long, uninterrupted presentation turns. Participants frequently overlap slightly around greetings, acknowledgments, and transitions, though substantive interruptions are uncommon. Speech is informal and supportive, marked by fillers and repairs such as “um,” “yeah,” “sort of,” “you know,” repeated words, self-corrections, and occasional fragmented starts. Questions tend to be friendly and prefaced with praise or hedges—“great talk,” “I have a naive question,” “I’m just curious”—then develop into multi-part exploratory prompts. Speakers build on prior comments by explicitly referring back to earlier points, often thinking aloud rather than sharply challenging claims. Disagreement or uncertainty is expressed indirectly through qualifications like “I don’t know,” “it could be,” “my prediction,” or “we haven’t looked at that,” and responses are generous, explanatory, and willing to acknowledge open questions.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - This might be a dumb question, but is that normal for this kind of data?
  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Choosing which retrofits to fund so older apartment buildings stay safe during multi-day heat waves.

speakers.name: Dr. Mei Lin
speakers.background: Dr. Lin is a building-performance engineer with 12 years of experience modeling heat resilience in multifamily housing. She has led energy audits and retrofit studies for municipal housing programs and uses whole-building simulation, weather files, indoor-temperature monitoring, and equipment-load calculations. For this project, she coordinates the common building list and has developed representative five-story-building simulations for a four-day heat-wave scenario.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Lin treats the retrofit decision as a constrained design and performance problem. She wants comparable package-level outputs from the building models, especially maximum indoor temperature, cooling load, and electrical demand under a specified heat-wave scenario. She is inclined to propose a clear indoor-temperature target, while recognizing that the health interpretation of modeled exposure should be supplied by public-health colleagues and the distributional implications by economics.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Amara Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a public-health researcher with 10 years of experience studying heat illness, emergency-care use, and housing-related environmental exposures in urban neighborhoods. Her work combines de-identified emergency-department records, age-stratified surveillance data, resident surveys, and community-based interpretation of barriers to protective actions. She has worked with older adults, people with chronic illness, and renters who cannot readily leave overheated apartments or use cooling centers.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Okafor frames risk as cumulative and unevenly distributed rather than as a single building-level temperature outcome. She focuses on nighttime conditions, the duration of elevated indoor heat, age-related vulnerability, ability to leave home, and whether residents can actually use available cooling. She expects modeled indoor conditions to be linked cautiously to population health evidence and is alert to metrics that can obscure high-risk residents behind a simple average or peak threshold.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Javier Reyes
speakers.background: Dr. Reyes is an urban and energy economist in his third postdoctoral year, following six years of doctoral research on residential energy burdens and landlord-tenant investment decisions. He builds cost-effectiveness and incidence models using capital-cost estimates, utility-bill projections, lease and ownership data, and policy uptake assumptions. For the retrofit program, he is assembling preliminary estimates of installation costs, operating savings, panel-upgrade requirements, and how benefits and costs fall on tenants versus building owners.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Reyes views the funding choice as a resource-allocation problem in which health outcomes are important but not the only consequence. He examines capital cost, electricity bills, avoided service use, implementation feasibility, landlord-tenant split incentives, and who receives benefits or bears costs. He prefers transparent comparisons that make distributional tradeoffs visible rather than treating a single outcome measure as the complete funding objective.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

seed_spec.explicit_instruction:
Run a methods meeting in which the team reaches limited procedural agreement but leaves two substantive methodological differences unresolved. Dr. Lin should present a proposal to rank retrofit packages primarily by modeled reductions in maximum indoor temperature during a four-day design heat wave, with a target of keeping apartments below 30°C. Dr. Okafor should respond indirectly, through a question or a comment about public-health practice, indicating concern that a 30°C threshold and maximum-temperature metric do not adequately represent health risk because overnight heat, duration of exposure, resident age, and inability to leave home matter. Do not have Dr. Okafor state direct disagreement. This is the first indirect disagreement.

Dr. Reyes should then raise a second indirect disagreement, also phrased as a question or comment about economic practice rather than direct opposition. Dr. Reyes should question whether a ranking based on avoided emergency visits alone can serve as the funding objective, noting that standard economic evaluation also considers resident electricity costs, landlord incentives, and distribution of benefits and costs between tenants and owners. Do not have Dr. Reyes state direct disagreement.

The team may agree to use a common building list, examine four-day heat-wave scenarios, and circulate available data. They must not resolve either methodological difference, choose a final ranking metric, or claim that the participants agree on the proposed 30°C/max-temperature or avoided-emergency-visit approach. Keep the discussion grounded in the stated project and avoid invented literature citations.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …and the weather file is finally behaving, so that's a small victory. Anyway, thanks for making time. I thought today we could keep the first ranking framework pretty simple. Agree on the evidence we can compare across all 20 buildings, and flag what we shouldn't pretend is more certain than it is. I've got the four-day model outputs ready, but before we settle on a temperature screen, I'd especially like to hear what matters most in the health data, because I don't want us to…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: …for health, I’d want to keep the age stratification visible from the start. A single hottest indoor temperature can miss someone in a warm bedroom all night, especially an older resident who can’t readily leave. Mei, do your runs retain hourly apartment or bedroom temperatures overnight, and show how long conditions stay elevated?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: Mm, overnight is really important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: The runs retain hourly zone temperatures, including separate bedroom proxies, and I can report both the overnight minimum and the hours above a threshold, not just the daily maximum. One thing I saw already is that exterior shading helps the afternoon peak quite a lot, but the bedroom near dawn stays warm longer than I expected. Amara, for your age-stratified interpretation, is duration overnight the more useful measure?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Both are informative, but I wouldn’t call either one sufficient on its own. The overnight minimum tells us whether there’s any real recovery, and the hours elevated gets closer to cumulative exposure, and then we need to keep the age groups visible when we interpret those outputs. I’d be cautious about turning that straight into avoided ED visits until I check what geographic detail the records actually...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: Right, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: This might be a dumb question, Amara, but what would the records actually let us say about avoided emergency visits, versus just identifying which age groups and exposure patterns are more concerning? I'm asking because in an economic evaluation, I'm not sure avoided visits alone would capture the things the city has to weigh, like resident electricity bills, landlord incentives, and who is actually paying for the retrofit...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: …at this stage, probably the latter. I need to check the geographic resolution and the age bands before saying the records can credibly give us building-level, or rather, avoided visits. But they can keep us from treating all modeled exposure as equivalent. Older residents and people who cannot leave a hot unit are not carrying the same risk.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: That seems like the right boundary for the first pass. Mei, when a package brings down those overnight temperatures, do you also see cooling electricity and coincident peak demand moving down together, or are there cases where one improves and the other doesn’t? I’m asking because the bill savings in my preliminary numbers may not line up neatly with the grid-side, um, constraint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: They do not always move together. Efficient cooling can improve indoor recovery while raising coincident electrical demand if the existing equipment is undersized or residents had not been cooling much before. Shading and insulation usually reduce cooling load, but the magnitude, the magnitude varies with window operation and occupancy. For each package, I can keep maximum and overnight temperatures alongside cooling energy and peak demand, instead of folding them into one score too early.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: That makes the accounting a little awkward, but usefully so. In a few of the older buildings, the panel upgrade is large enough to flip the efficient-cooling package from looking cheap to expensive, depending on whether we treat it as shared infrastructure or charge it to that package. Before I start comparing dollar savings, I need to check whether owners can actually recover any of those, those capital costs through rents or operating charges.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …then I think we should leave the panel upgrade visible as a separate required cost and not let it disappear inside the cooling package. For the initial technical screen, I’d still use keeping modeled apartments below 30°C during the four-day heat wave, but report the overnight minimum and hours above 30°C alongside it. Amara, does 30°C work as a provisional reporting threshold, rather than, um, a claim of health protection?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: …as a reporting threshold, yes, as long as it stays a screen and not a pass/fail health finding. I’d want that same table to show whether bedrooms actually cool overnight and how many hours they stay above it, because a unit that briefly hits 30 and cools is not the same exposure as one that stays warm through the night. And for survey respondents with AC who still do not run it, we should not treat the modeled cooling package as automatic protection.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …yes, that is an important limitation. I can run the cooling cases with a modest-use assumption and a non-use or limited-use sensitivity case, rather than treating equipment installation as the same thing as actual cooling. And the 30°C screen should apply to the bedroom hours too, not just the apartment-wide maximum. Does that give you enough to distinguish the overnight concern in the first table?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: …yes, I think that gets us much closer. Could the limited-use case- could it distinguish daytime from overnight use, though? The survey pattern was people reporting AC access but sleeping through very warm nights without running it, and I don't know yet whether that's cost concern, noise, or something else. Treating all limited use the same might hide that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: Hm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …I can do that. I'll separate the operating schedules into daytime-only, overnight-only, and limited use across both periods, and then show how the bedroom temperatures and the electrical peak change. I do need to treat those as sensitivities, though, because until we know why residents aren't running AC at night, I shouldn't assume one schedule represents everyone, so…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: …and that may be exactly where the bill side enters. If daytime-only use produces acceptable afternoon temperatures but leaves bedrooms hot, and overnight operation changes the tenant's bill a lot, we should show that rather than assume the equipment is being used wrong. I don't yet know whether the survey can tell us anything about who is most, most constrained by those operating costs, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: …right, and I’d be careful about treating the bill sensitivity as just an average tenant bill. If the survey can’t tell us who’s constrained, we can at least label that uncertainty and keep the daytime and overnight results separate, because the people least able to absorb added summer cost may also be the ones who aren’t getting overnight recovery.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: Yeah, I see.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …and that's also why I don't want just one cooling-package result. I can put the three operating schedules next to the no-cooling case, with bedroom overnight hours above 30°C, cooling energy, and coincident peak. Then Javier, could your bill ranges be attached to those schedules instead of just to installed equipment? I still need to test how much window opening changes that shading result, too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: …yeah, I can attach provisional tenant bill ranges to each schedule, but I'd keep the panel cost separate in the same table. A low operating bill can make the cooling option look attractive, but then the required electrical work is- it can end up sitting off to the side. And I need to check the lease terms before we imply owners can pass any of that through.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …yes, that seems like the cleanest way to present it. I’ll keep the panel work separate as a building-specific requirement, and I’ll flag where the model is sensitive to window opening, occupancy, and outages, rather than suggesting the representative run transfers perfectly. Javier, with the different existing equipment, we should probably note how stable those panel estimates are, since…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: …yes, I think that needs a caveat. The estimates are provisional, and they’re probably most stable on whether a panel upgrade is needed at all, not on the exact cost. Service capacity, existing loads, and local electrical conditions can move it a lot. I’d show a range and maybe mark the buildings where panel work is the ranking-changing uncertainty, rather than treating it like a precise package price.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, worth flagging.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: …yes. I think that keeps it honest. For each building, panel work would be a separate flag with a cost range, and we can show whether that range changes the package ordering. I’ll make the technical table explicit about the 30°C screen, overnight bedroom exposure, the three use schedules, and the sensitivities, so we’re not collapsing either the health or the cost interpretation too soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Javier Reyes
transcript.text: I think we should leave it there—this was really helpful. I’ll follow up by email once I’ve checked the lease- the lease issue. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: All right. Thank you both—talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, take care, both.

issues: The transcript partially resolves what the seed requires to remain unresolved. In turns 12-15, Lin proposes 30°C only as a provisional reporting screen and Okafor accepts that framing; in turns 21-26, the team converges on a multi-column presentation with schedules, exposure measures, bill ranges, and panel-cost flags. Although no final single ranking metric is selected, this is stronger procedural/methodological convergence than the requested limited agreement and makes the two substantive disputes less clearly unresolved.

Naturalness is limited by the highly polished, agenda-efficient construction of most substantive turns. For example, turns 10-15 and 21-26 repeatedly turn each concern directly into a specific modeling change, assignment, or tidy shared framing. The disfluencies are present but often appear as surface repairs within otherwise complete, well-structured arguments.
